_note: PARK ROAD CORRECTIONS, FROM PHOTOGRAPHS. The owner's rule: trust OSM for WHERE, photographs for WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. 'OSM is right about the road and trail LOCATIONS, but often very wrong about the style, eg specifying a multilane road when it's barely a 1-lane with a side trail (not a sidewalk).' So the geometry is never touched here and the STYLE is corrected: how wide the carriageway really is, whether there is a kerb and on which side, whether a detached trail runs alongside and what it is made of, and what built objects exist. Written once from pictures and then applied deterministically at bake time and at render time, in the spirit of docs/devices/quirks.yaml - encode the answer, do not re-decide it. See docs/PARKS.md and docs/GGP-GRID.md.
_keyedByName: Keyed by NAME, not by way id, and that is a deliberate departure from the brief. Martin Luther King Junior Drive is 105 baked edges across four OSM highway classes; John F. Kennedy Drive is 70. A park road's character is consistent over long runs - which is the owner's own argument for why photographing a handful of points is enough - so one row per drive is the unit the evidence actually supports, and a table of 300 way ids would be 300 rows of the same answer going stale independently. `ways` on a row pins it to specific OSM ids where a drive genuinely changes character along its length; nothing needs it yet.
_applied: ONLY INSIDE THE PARK MASK (city/park-area.ts), so a street of the same name outside open country is untouched. `width` replaces the park's blanket cap for that road; everything else is recorded evidence that the renderer does not consume yet, and each such field says so below. A row with no `width` still earns its place: it is the photograph's answer, written down, so the next agent does not go and look again.

_fields.match: the way's OSM `name`, exactly as it is tagged (both spellings of a name that OSM spells two ways get their own rows)
_fields.kind: optional: only apply to ways whose OSM `highway` is this. A drive that is `tertiary` for cars and `pedestrian` where it is closed to them is two different places with one name.
_fields.ways: optional: OSM way ids, when a row is meant for part of a drive rather than all of it
_fields.width: the CARRIAGEWAY in metres, measured off the photograph against a known width (a US traffic lane is 3.0-3.7 m, a parked car 1.8 m). Applied.
_fields.kerb: none | left | right | both, in the direction the OSM way is drawn. NOT APPLIED YET: the kerb renderer draws both sides or neither. Recorded because it is the single most park-like fact in the references and the renderer should grow a side.
_fields.trail: none | left | right | both - is there a DETACHED path alongside, a few metres off through the grass? It is already its own OSM way with its own geometry, so this is a verification note, not a thing to synthesise. NOT APPLIED.
_fields.trailSurface: asphalt | dirt | concrete, from the photograph. NOT APPLIED.
_fields.objects: what is actually built along it, from the photograph. The park's answer is almost always 'nothing'.
_fields.evidence: the Mapillary frame id (tools/cache/mapillary/pano-<id>.jpg) or the reference file it was read off
_fields.at: where that photograph was taken, lat lon
_fields.square: which square of docs/ggp-grid.csv it falls in
_fields.status: photographed (somebody looked at a picture of THIS road) | inferred (read across from a photographed road of the same character) | unverified (nobody has looked; a guess from OSM alone)

roads.objects: one classic cast-iron lamppost on the verge between road and trail; a small blue plate on a post; nothing else
roads._note: At the Queen Wilhelmina Garden. Two lanes with kerbside parking, so nine metres of asphalt rather than the 12.6 m OSM's classification implies - and the kerb is on the garden side ONLY. On the other side the grass verge runs straight off the asphalt to a SEPARATE asphalt path two or three metres away. Exactly the MLK pattern of docs/PARKS.md, photographed on a second road, which is what makes it a rule rather than one road's quirk. CORROBORATED mid-park by frame 3488211868164573 at 37.77160 -122.48957, which is the pattern entire in one frame: carriageway, no kerb, a bare brown DUFF strip of eucalyptus bark and leaf litter - not grass - then a detached asphalt trail two or three metres off, and one classic lamppost carrying a small plate. Two photographed points four hundred metres apart agreeing is what makes this a rule for the whole drive rather than a reading of one spot.

OSM spells this drive both ways; same road, same answer. East end, near the Conservatory: two lanes and kerbside parking both sides, and on the north side NO KERB AT ALL - the asphalt gives way to a gravel-and-dirt shoulder, then California poppies and dense shrub understorey, then eucalyptus and Monterey pine. The detached asphalt path runs behind the parked cars. One yellow warning diamond is the only sign in the frame.

roads.evidence: OSM geometry + the character of JFK Drive either side of it
roads._note: THE ONE ROW THAT MAKES THE ROAD WIDER RATHER THAN NARROWER, and it is why the park's blanket trail cap was wrong. The Promenade is the former JFK carriageway closed to cars - it is baked as `pedestrian`, so `foot` is true, so the park rule capped it at 3.0 m when OSM had it at up to 19.4 m. Neither number is the place: it is a two-lane road that people ride on, about twelve metres wide. A trail cap must not be applied to a way that is a road in everything but its access tag.

roads.objects: plain timber bollards; a short run of metal barrier
roads._note: Same case as the JFK Promenade: closed to cars, tagged `pedestrian`, and it is a road. The purest example of the park's character - one narrow strip of worn asphalt, NO KERB ANYWHERE, the surface giving way straight to a dirt-and-leaf shoulder, then undergrowth, then trunks, with the canopy closing right over. Keeping its mapped eight metres rather than capping it to three is what lets it read as the photograph.

roads.objects: a STOP sign and a small green street-name blade at the junction; one classic lamppost with a 25 mph plate along the runs
roads._note: PHOTOGRAPHED NOW, and the reference shot's reading held: two narrow lanes, kerb on ONE side only - the far side carries a kerb line with grass above it while the near side gives straight onto a dirt-and-grass shoulder - with dense green understorey and white flowering shrub right up to the edge. OSM bakes it at up to 16 m across four highway classes; it is seven. THE ONE SURPRISE is the junction: there IS a red stop sign and a small green name blade there, in a park whose brief says 'there are almost no signs'. Both are true - nothing along the runs, ordinary signing where two drives meet. That photograph is why `stop` went back into `default.park.keepFurniture`.

roads.evidence: mapillary 228965076269626 (24 m off the drive); read across from MLK Drive; OSM carries Transverse Drive Path and Transverse Drive Trail beside it
OSM: `highway=secondary`, four lanes, part of California SR 1
roads._note: THE EXCEPTION THAT PROVES THE PARK RULE, and the reason the through-road exemption exists in park-area.ts. Crossover Drive is State Route 1 crossing Golden Gate Park: a real four-lane highway that happens to run through open country, and capping it to a 6.5 m park lane makes it a footpath. Note for anyone applying the brief literally - it is tagged `secondary`, NOT `primary` or `trunk`, so an exemption written for those two alone would not have caught it. The exemption is on classified through-routes as a class. STILL UNVERIFIED AFTER THE TOKEN, and this is now a coverage fact rather than an access one. Mapillary's park imagery is overwhelmingly cyclists and walkers on the drives and trails; two attempts to sample the Crossover carriageway returned the nearest frames from the park lanes BESIDE it - a narrow two-lane road with no kerb, a dirt shoulder and a detached path, which is emphatically not a four-lane state highway. Rather than read those frames as Crossover and record a wrong answer confidently, the row stays on its OSM evidence. Anyone finishing it should look for a dashcam or survey sequence on SR 1, of the kind frame 372808759228160 is on the Great Highway.

roads.objects: tall modern mast street lighting, signals, highway signage, guard rail - NOT classic park lampposts
roads._note: PHOTOGRAPHED, and it settles the through-route exemption by showing what the exemption is FOR: a four-lane divided arterial with a yellow centre line, kerbs both sides and tall modern mast lighting. Nothing about it is a park lane and capping it to 6.5 m would have made a state highway into a footpath. The lighting is the detail that earned its own rule - the classic ornate cast-iron post would be as wrong here as a parking meter is on Middle Drive, so the park's lamppost planting now skips a road this wide. ALSO, and this is the #200 evidence: the dunes come right up to the western kerb, deep dry SAND with dune grass on it, exactly where we render bright mown lawn today.

roads.evidence: OSM width; consistent with every mapped park path in the package
read across from Middle Drive: same class, same part of the park, same forested character

roads.objects: nothing whatever - no kerb, no lamppost, no sign, no post
roads._note: PHOTOGRAPHED, and it confirms Middle Drive West's reading on the other half of the same road: one narrow two-lane strip with a painted white edge line and NO KERB ANYWHERE, the asphalt giving straight onto a grass verge strewn with fallen eucalyptus bark, then a DIRT trail a few metres off through the grass, then dense shrub, then trunks. The only marking is on the road itself. Nothing is built along it at all, which is the strongest single statement of the park's character in any frame taken so far.
